title: Arise, shine (Isaiah 60:1)
hookLine: "Arise, shine, for thy light is come"
carry: the light came before you did

cards: Wake up, wake up, for your light has come. That line is sung on Friday night in Lecha Dodi, the song that welcomes Shabbat like a bride, in a verse that calls out to a city. Inside it sit two Hebrew words: kumi ori.
Arise, shine. They weren't written for the song. The poet borrowed them from Isaiah, from the opening of chapter sixty, where the prophet calls out to a city sitting in the dark.

teach.h: SPOKEN TO ZION, IN THE DUST.
teach.b: Chapter sixty opens: "Arise, shine; for thy light is come, and the glory of the LORD is risen upon thee." The one spoken to is Zion, the city, pictured as a woman.
A few chapters earlier, Isaiah told her to shake herself from the dust. Now she's told to stand up. And look at the tense.
Thy light is come. Not will come. Not might come if you try hard enough.
It has come. The command to rise arrives after the light, not before it. She isn't told to make the morning, only to get up into a morning that's already here.
The next verse is honest about the world around her: darkness shall cover the earth, and gross darkness the people. The night isn't over everywhere.

But the light is on her, in the middle of that darkness, and others will come toward it: nations shall come to thy light, and kings to the brightness of thy rising. And the order matters. Arise comes first, shine second.
You can't shine lying down. The first act is simply standing up. That's why the line fits a Friday night so well.
The week may have been dark and heavy.
But Shabbat has come in, and the song says: get up.

how: Isaiah 60 is among the prophetic readings of comfort after Tisha B'Av, and its opening words, kumi ori, are sung on Friday nights in the Shabbat song Lecha Dodi.

o: rest: a call to lie still and wait
stand up: the first word of Isaiah sixty
shine: to give off light like the sun

p: the song that borrows the line

s: the verse says the light will come if Zion rises
thy light is come: the light arrives first, then the call to rise.
the next verse admits darkness still covers the earth
darkness shall cover the earth, and the light is on Zion in the middle of it.
kumi ori was written for Lecha Dodi
the song borrows the words from Isaiah 60.

games.q: you're Zion, sitting in the dust. darkness still covers the earth. what does the verse ask of you?
o: wait until the whole world is light.
arise, shine, for thy light is come.
stay down until you feel ready.
games.why: "arise, shine; for thy light is come." the light is already here; the first act is standing up.

practice: Sit up a little taller, or stand, and let one thing that's already good in this day come to mind: light through a window, coffee, a person, a small piece of good news. It's here already, and you don't have to earn it; let it land.
If you pray, you can hold the verse: arise, shine, for thy light is come.
